findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body: When callers invoke the returned disposer, the newly registered `"message"` handler remains attached. Subsequent messages can invoke stale callbacks, while repeated attach/dispose cycles retain handlers and increase memory use and dispatch work. The prior implementation called `socket.off("message", handler)`; the replacement is an empty function.

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the disposer no longer unregisters `handler`. Any later `"message"` event still invokes supposedly detached handlers, causing stale callbacks, duplicate processing after reattachment, and listener leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
Calling the disposer returned by `attach` no longer unregisters `handler`. Any later `"message"` still invokes a supposedly detached handler, and repeated attach/dispose cycles accumulate listeners, causing duplicate processing and leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the disposer no longer removes the `"message"` handler. A remote peer that can emit messages after session teardown can continue invoking stale handlers, bypassing the intended lifecycle boundary; repeated attach/dispose cycles also accumulate handlers and amplify attacker-controlled messages into memory/CPU exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the returned cleanup function no longer unregisters the `"message"` listener. Repeated attach/cleanup cycles on a long-lived socket retain every handler and its captured state, causing unbounded memory growth and increasing per-message dispatch cost.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
